title: The other gods of the Bible
question: Who were Baal, Asherah, Astarte, Dagon, Chemosh, Molech, Marduk and the other gods the Bible names? Why were Israelites so often drawn to them, how does the Bible treat them, and what happened to them in the end?
plainAnswer: The Bible was written in a world full of gods. Every nation around Israel had its own: Baal the storm god who brought rain, Asherah and Astarte the great goddesses, Dagon the grain god of the Philistines, Chemosh of Moab, Molech and Milcom of Ammon, Marduk and Nabu of Babylon, and many more. Israel was told to worship Yahweh alone, but many Israelites, including kings, also turned to these gods, usually for practical reasons: rain, harvests, children, political alliances and family custom. The prophets fought back by mocking the gods, rewriting their names as insults, and telling stories in which they are humiliated. Archaeology has confirmed many of these gods and some of the practices the Bible condemns. After Josiah's reform and the exile, Jewish faith became firmly devoted to one God, and later Jewish and Christian writers came to see the old gods as idols with demonic powers behind them.
keyTakeaways: Most of the gods the Bible names are well known from ancient texts and archaeology; they were not invented by the biblical writers.
Baal mattered because Canaan depended on rain; the contest on Mount Carmel is a storm-god contest won by Yahweh on Baal's own terms.
Biblical writers deliberately distorted some names: Ashtoreth, Molech and Ish-bosheth all carry the vowels or word for 'shame' (bosheth).
Some popular ideas are wrong: Dagon was a grain god, not a fish god; 'Baal' is a title meaning 'lord', not a personal name.
Inscriptions such as Kuntillet Ajrud ('Yahweh and his asherah') show how widespread mixed worship was; what they mean is debated.
Josiah's purge and the Babylonian exile ended the worship of other gods as a mainstream option in Judaism.
In later Jewish and Christian thought the old gods were understood as idols behind which demons stood (Deut 32:17; 1 Cor 10:20).

sections.heading: A world full of gods
sections.body:
Ancient peoples did not ask whether gods existed; they asked which gods ruled where, and how to keep them happy. Each nation had a chief god who protected its land and king, and each household might honour smaller gods of family, fertility and the dead. Gods were tied to places: Chemosh ruled Moab, Milcom ruled Ammon, Dagon was honoured in the Philistine cities. That is why Jephthah could say to the Ammonites, 'Wilt not thou possess that which Chemosh thy god giveth thee?' (Judg 11:24), and why Naaman took two mule-loads of Israelite soil home so that he could worship Israel's God in Syria (2 Kgs 5:17).

The Bible's first commandment is spoken into this world: 'Thou shalt have no other gods before me' (Exod 20:3). Israel was not to add Yahweh to a collection of gods, as its neighbours did, but to worship him alone. Much of the Old Testament is the story of how hard Israel found this.

Scholars disagree about how these gods were understood. Some see them as purely human inventions that the Bible ridicules; others, following texts such as Deut 32:8-9 and Ps 82, think the biblical writers believed real spiritual powers stood behind the nations' gods. The guide on the divine council covers that question; this guide focuses on who the gods were and how Israel met them.

sections.heading: Baal: the storm god and the problem of rain
sections.body:
'Baal' is not really a name. It is a common word meaning 'lord', 'owner' or 'husband'. The god behind the title was Hadad (Haddu), the storm god of Syria and Canaan, who brought thunder, lightning and rain. In the Ugaritic texts discovered from 1928–29 at Ras Shamra on the Syrian coast, Baal lives on Mount Zaphon (Jebel Aqra, near the modern Syrian–Turkish border), defeats Yam, the chaotic Sea, with clubs made by the craftsman god Kothar-wa-Khasis, gets a palace, and then goes down to Mot, Death. While he is dead the land dries up. His violent sister Anat kills Mot, and Baal returns, bringing back the rains. Many scholars read this as reflecting the yearly cycle of dry summer and wet winter, though the exact link is debated.

This explains Baal's pull on Israel. Egypt had the Nile and Mesopotamia had great rivers, but the land of Canaan 'drinketh water of the rain of heaven' (Deut 11:10-11). A failed rainy season meant famine. Hosea complains that Israel credited Baal with the grain, wine and oil that Yahweh had given (Hos 2:8). Biblical poetry pointedly gives Yahweh Baal's own titles and imagery: he is the one who 'rideth upon the heavens' (Ps 68:4), makes the clouds his chariot (Ps 104:3), and thunders over the waters (Ps 29:3).

The showdown on Mount Carmel (1 Kgs 18) is a storm-god contest. Under Ahab and his Phoenician queen Jezebel, 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah ate at the royal table (1 Kgs 18:19). After three years of drought Elijah challenges them to call down fire. The prophets cry out and cut themselves, possibly a mourning rite for a dying god; Elijah mocks Baal as musing, busy (probably a polite way of saying 'relieving himself'), travelling or asleep (1 Kgs 18:27). Then Elijah has the altar soaked with twelve jars of water, fire falls, and the rain returns (1 Kgs 18:45). Yahweh wins on Baal's home ground: fire from heaven and rain.

Local forms of Baal appear too: Baal-peor, where Israel sinned with Moab and 24,000 died (Num 25:1-9), remembered for centuries (Hos 9:10; Ps 106:28); and Baal-berith, 'lord of the covenant', at Shechem (Judg 8:33). Jeremiah was still condemning Baal worship nearly three hundred years after Elijah (Jer 11:13).

sources.author: Mark S. Smith
sources.title: The Ugaritic Baal Cycle, vol. 1

sources.author: John Day

callout.text: Myth: 'Baal was one god called Baal.' Fact: 'baal' means 'lord' and was used of many gods and local forms of gods. In the Bible it usually means the storm god Hadad, but 'the Baals' (plural, Judg 2:11) can refer to a whole range of local deities.

sections.heading: Asherah and Astarte: the goddesses
sections.body:
Asherah was the great mother goddess of Canaan. At Ugarit she is Athirat, 'Lady Athirat of the Sea', wife of the high god El and mother of the gods, said to have seventy sons. In the Bible the word asherah means two things: the goddess herself (1 Kgs 18:19; 2 Kgs 23:4) and a wooden cult object, a pole or stylised tree, that could be planted, cut down and burned (Deut 16:21; Judg 6:25-26). King Manasseh even set up a carved image of Asherah in Yahweh's temple (2 Kgs 21:7), and there were rooms where women wove hangings for her (2 Kgs 23:7).

Inscriptions have made Asherah famous. At Kuntillet Ajrud in north-east Sinai, excavated in 1975–76, storage jars from about 800 BC carry blessings 'by Yahweh of Samaria and his asherah' and 'by Yahweh of Teman and his asherah'. A tomb inscription from Khirbet el-Qom near Hebron has similar wording. Scholars disagree about what 'his asherah' means. Hebrew does not normally add 'his' to a personal name, so some argue it means Yahweh's cult symbol, the wooden pole; others think ordinary Israelites saw Asherah as Yahweh's consort. Either way, it shows that many Israelites combined Yahweh with Asherah or her symbol, exactly what the prophets condemned.

Astarte (Hebrew Ashtoreth, plural Ashtaroth) was a goddess of love, fertility and war, the western cousin of the Mesopotamian Ishtar. She was the city goddess of Sidon; Sidonian royal inscriptions name kings and a queen mother as her priests. Solomon built a high place for 'Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians' (1 Kgs 11:5); after the Philistines killed Saul they put his armour in 'the house of Ashtaroth' (1 Sam 31:10). The 'Queen of Heaven', to whom the women of Judah baked cakes (Jer 7:18; Jer 44:17-19), was probably Astarte, Ishtar, or a blend of the two; scholars debate which.

callout.text: Did Yahweh have a wife? Some scholars (for example William Dever) argue that popular religion paired Yahweh with Asherah as his consort. Others (for example Judith Hadley, on a cautious reading) think 'his asherah' refers to a cult object linked to Yahweh. All agree the Bible's writers rejected any such pairing.

sections.heading: Gods of the neighbours: Dagon, Baal-zebub, Chemosh and Molech
sections.body:
Dagon (Dagan) was the god of the Philistines' cities Ashdod and Gaza (Judg 16:23; 1 Sam 5:2). He was not a fish god. That idea comes from the Hebrew word dag ('fish') and was popularised by medieval Jewish commentators. In fact Dagan was an old Syrian grain and land god, honoured at Ebla and Mari in the third millennium BC; dagan is also the ordinary Hebrew word for grain. At Ugarit Baal is called 'son of Dagan'. The Philistines, who came from the Aegean, adopted him. When they put the captured ark of God in his temple at Ashdod (about 1050 BC), the statue fell on its face twice; the second time its head and hands were broken off on the threshold, which is why Dagon's priests would not tread on it (1 Sam 5:3-5). Samson died pulling down Dagon's temple at Gaza (Judg 16:23-30), and Saul's head was hung in Dagon's temple (1 Chr 10:10).

Baal-zebub, 'lord of flies', was the god of Ekron whom King Ahaziah consulted after a fall (2 Kgs 1:2-3). Ugaritic texts call Baal zbl, 'prince', so the original was probably Baal-zebul, 'Baal the Prince'; changing one letter turned a royal title into an insult. By Jesus' day Beelzebul was a name for the prince of demons (Matt 12:24; Mark 3:22). An inscription found at Ekron in 1996 names the city's kings Achish (Ikausu) and Padi, known from Assyrian records, and a goddess called Ptgyh, otherwise unknown.

Chemosh was the national god of Moab; the Moabites are 'the people of Chemosh' (Num 21:29). The Mesha Stele, found at Dhiban in 1868, is a royal inscription of about 840 BC in which King Mesha says Omri of Israel oppressed Moab 'because Chemosh was angry with his land', then that Chemosh told him to take Nebo from Israel, and that he dragged 'the vessels of Yahweh' before Chemosh. It mirrors the Bible's theology from the other side. When Mesha sacrificed his firstborn son on the city wall, 'there was great indignation against Israel' and Israel withdrew (2 Kgs 3:27); interpreters disagree whether this means Chemosh's anger, Yahweh's, or Israel's own horror.

Molech is linked with the burning of children 'through the fire' at Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem (Lev 18:21; 2 Kgs 23:10; Jer 32:35). The name's consonants mlk mean 'king'; Milcom, god of Ammon, shares the same root (1 Kgs 11:5; 1 Kgs 11:7). In 1935 Otto Eissfeldt argued from Punic inscriptions that molk was a type of sacrifice rather than a god's name; scholars such as George Heider and John Day replied that a deity is meant. The Valley of Hinnom (Ge-hinnom) later gave its name to Gehenna, the word Jesus uses for hell (Matt 5:22; Mark 9:43).

callout.text: Myth: 'Dagon was a half-fish god.' Fact: the fish idea comes from a medieval word-play on Hebrew dag, 'fish'. The ancient Dagan was a grain and land god known long before the Philistines arrived.

sections.heading: Gods of the empires
sections.body:
When Assyria and Babylon conquered the region, their gods came too. Marduk, chief god of Babylon, is called Bel ('lord') and Merodach in the Bible; his son Nabu, god of writing and wisdom, appears as Nebo, and both names were built into royal names such as Nebuchadnezzar and Merodach-baladan. Isaiah pictures the idols of Bel and Nebo loaded onto weary animals as Babylon falls: gods who must be carried, while Yahweh carries his people (Isa 46:1-4; Jer 50:2).

After Assyria deported the northern kingdom in 722 BC, it resettled Samaria with people from elsewhere, who brought their own gods: Succoth-benoth from Babylon, Nergal from Cuth, Ashima from Hamath, Nibhaz and Tartak from the Avvites, and Adrammelech and Anammelech, to whom the Sepharvites burned their children (2 Kgs 17:29-31). Nergal was indeed the plague and underworld god of Cuthah, so the writer matched god and city correctly. Sennacherib was killed while worshipping in the house of Nisroch (2 Kgs 19:37), a god not yet securely identified.

In Ezekiel's vision, women sit at the temple gate 'weeping for Tammuz' (Ezek 8:14), the Mesopotamian shepherd god Dumuzi, lover of Inanna/Ishtar, mourned each year; and twenty-five men turn their backs on the temple to worship the sun (Ezek 8:16). Further afield the Bible meets Egypt's gods, whom God judges in the exodus (Exod 12:12; Num 33:4), and in the New Testament the Greek gods: Paul and Barnabas are hailed as Zeus and Hermes (Acts 14:11-13), and Ephesus riots over Artemis (Acts 19:23-41).

sections.heading: Why Israel was tempted
sections.body:
It is easy to read the Old Testament and wonder why Israel kept turning to other gods. But the reasons were practical and often understandable. First, rain and food: in a land that lived or died by the rainy season, it felt safer to honour the god everyone else said controlled the storms (Hos 2:5; Hos 2:8). Second, fertility: families wanted children and healthy herds, and goddesses such as Asherah and Astarte were associated with birth and abundance. Thousands of small clay female figurines found in Judahite houses of the eighth and seventh centuries BC probably served such household hopes, though what exactly they represent is debated.

Third, politics: royal marriages brought foreign gods to court. Solomon's foreign wives led him to build shrines for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom (1 Kgs 11:1-8), and Ahab's marriage to Jezebel of Sidon brought Baal worship to Samaria (1 Kgs 16:31-33). Treaties with powerful empires could include honouring their gods (2 Kgs 16:10-16). Fourth, family religion: household gods (teraphim) appear in the homes of Rachel and of Michal (Gen 31:19; 1 Sam 19:13), and Jeremiah's opponents defend the Queen of Heaven as the custom of 'our fathers, our kings, and our princes' (Jer 44:17).

The refugees in Egypt put the argument plainly: 'since we left off to burn incense to the queen of heaven… we have wanted all things' (Jer 44:18). To them, the reform had failed and the old ways worked. The prophets answered that the disasters came precisely because Israel had abandoned its covenant God (Jer 44:22-23).

sources.author: Rainer Albertz
sources.title: A History of Israelite Religion in the Old Testament Period

sources.author: Raz Kletter
sources.title: The Judean Pillar-Figurines and the Archaeology of Asherah

sections.heading: How the Bible mocks and renames the gods
sections.body:
Biblical writers did not treat other gods politely. They mocked them. Idols have mouths but cannot speak and eyes but cannot see (Ps 115:4-8). Isaiah describes a man who cuts down a tree, burns half of it to roast meat and warm himself, then carves the other half into a god and prays to it, 'Deliver me; for thou art my god' (Isa 44:13-20). Jeremiah compares idols to scarecrows in a cucumber field (Jer 10:5). Elijah suggests Baal may be asleep or on the toilet (1 Kgs 18:27).

They also changed names. The Hebrew word bosheth means 'shame', and scribes sometimes replaced 'Baal' with it or gave a god's name the vowels of bosheth. Saul's son Eshbaal ('man of Baal', 1 Chr 8:33) becomes Ish-bosheth ('man of shame', 2 Sam 2:8); Jonathan's son Merib-baal (1 Chr 8:34) becomes Mephibosheth (2 Sam 4:4); Gideon's name Jerubbaal (Judg 6:32) becomes Jerubbesheth (2 Sam 11:21). The goddess Ashtart becomes Ashtoreth, and melek ('king') becomes Molech, both probably by inserting the vowels of bosheth. Jeremiah calls Baal's altars 'altars to that shameful thing' (Jer 11:13).

Places were renamed too. The hill east of Jerusalem where Solomon built shrines to Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom is called 'the mount of corruption' (2 Kgs 23:13), probably a one-letter pun on 'Mount of Anointing', an old name for the Mount of Olives. And Baal-zebul, 'Baal the Prince', becomes Baal-zebub, 'lord of flies' (2 Kgs 1:2). A good rule of thumb: when a biblical name looks odd, check whether the scribes changed it on purpose. Not every such explanation is certain, so scholars weigh each case.

callout.text: Not every 'Baal' name was pagan. In Saul's and David's time, baal ('lord') could be used of Yahweh himself, which is why loyal Israelites gave their sons Baal names. Hosea later forbids calling Yahweh 'my Baal' (Hos 2:16), and scribes then changed the old names.

sections.heading: What archaeology has found
sections.body:
Archaeology has confirmed many of the gods and practices the Bible describes, and complicated some assumptions. The Ugaritic tablets from Ras Shamra (excavated from 1929 and written in an alphabetic cuneiform deciphered in 1930) give the myths of El, Baal, Anat and Athirat in Canaanite form. The Mesha Stele (found 1868; broken by local people in 1869 and reconstructed from fragments and a paper squeeze made by Charles Clermont-Ganneau) gives Moab's account of Chemosh and contains one of the earliest mentions of Yahweh outside the Bible.

Inside Israel and Judah, the inscriptions of Kuntillet Ajrud and Khirbet el-Qom link Yahweh with 'his asherah'. At Tel Arad, a Judahite fortress in the Negev, a small shrine had standing stones and two limestone altars; a 2020 analysis of residue found frankincense mixed with animal fat on one and cannabis on the other, from the eighth century BC. The shrine was deliberately buried, perhaps during Hezekiah's or Josiah's reforms; the date is debated. At Ekron a 1996 inscription names the temple builders and their goddess Ptgyh.

The tophet at Carthage, a Phoenician colony, contains thousands of urns of burned infants and young animals with stelae dedicated to Baal Hammon and Tanit, used over several centuries. Greek and Roman writers such as Diodorus Siculus (Library 20.14) described child sacrifice there. Whether these were sacrifices or a cemetery for infants who died naturally is debated: a 2010 study argued many were stillborn or newborn natural deaths, while later studies argued the age pattern fits sacrifice. Either way, it shows the kind of rite the Bible condemns at Topheth.

sources.author: André Lemaire
sources.title: "House of David" Restored in Moabite Inscription (Biblical Archaeology Review 20/3)

sections.heading: Josiah's purge and the exile
sections.body:
The most thorough attack on the other gods came under King Josiah of Judah, around 622–621 BC, after a 'book of the law' was found in the temple (2 Kgs 22:8). Josiah burned the vessels made for Baal, Asherah and 'all the host of heaven' outside Jerusalem; removed the priests who burned incense to Baal, the sun, the moon and the constellations; took the Asherah out of the temple, burned it at the Kidron, ground it to powder and scattered the dust on common graves; broke down the houses of the cult prostitutes where women wove for Asherah; defiled Topheth so that no one could burn a child there; removed the horses dedicated to the sun and burned the chariots of the sun; and destroyed Solomon's shrines to Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom (2 Kgs 23:4-14).

The reform did not last. Jeremiah and Ezekiel still condemn idolatry after Josiah's death (Jer 44; Ezek 8). But the Babylonian conquest in 586 BC changed everything. In the ancient view, a defeated nation's god had lost. The prophets argued the opposite: Yahweh had used Babylon to judge his people, and he was not tied to a land. Ezekiel saw God's glory by a canal in Babylon (Ezek 1:1-28), and Second Isaiah (Isa 40–48, written in the exile according to most scholars) declared that the gods of Babylon were nothing and that Yahweh alone controlled history (Isa 44:6-8; Isa 46:1-2).

After the exile, the worship of other gods largely disappears as a mainstream option within Judaism. The struggles of the Maccabean period were against Greek religion imposed from outside, not against Baal or Asherah. How far the exile created this change, and how far it confirmed an older faith, is part of the debate on monotheism in Israel.

callout.text: Scholars disagree about how much of 2 Kings 23 describes what Josiah actually did and how much reflects later idealising. Many think the core reform is historical; some think its scale has been enlarged. Archaeology (for example the buried Arad shrine) can be read either way.

sections.heading: From gods to demons, and what it means today
sections.body:
Even before the exile, some texts say that the nations' gods were really 'devils' (shedim, demons): Israel 'sacrificed unto devils, not to God; to gods whom they knew not' (Deut 32:17; compare Ps 106:37 and the goat-demons of Lev 17:7). When Jewish scholars translated the Bible into Greek (the Septuagint), they rendered 'all the gods of the nations are idols' in Ps 96:5 as 'all the gods of the nations are demons' (daimonia). Paul combines both ideas: an idol is nothing (1 Cor 8:4), yet what pagans sacrifice they offer 'to devils, and not to God' (1 Cor 10:20). Revelation speaks of people who 'worship devils, and idols of gold' (Rev 9:20).

Later tradition went further. Beelzebul became the prince of demons in the Gospels (Mark 3:22). Medieval and early modern magical books made Astaroth (Astarte, now male) a duke of hell, and John Milton's *Paradise Lost* (1667, book 1) gave a whole catalogue of fallen angels named after Old Testament gods: Moloch, Chemosh, Baalim and Ashtaroth, Thammuz, Dagon, Rimmon. These are literary and folk developments, not biblical teaching, but they show how the gods of Canaan lived on in the Christian imagination.

What does it mean today? Most Christians and Jews do not face statues of Baal. But the reasons Israel turned to other gods are familiar: security, prosperity, fertility, political advantage, family habit. The New Testament applies the idea of idolatry to greed (Col 3:5) and to anything that takes God's place (1 John 5:21); Jesus warns that no one can serve God and mammon (Matt 6:24). Paul's speech in Athens shows another side: he engages respectfully with people who worship 'an unknown god' and proclaims the Creator to them (Acts 17:22-31). The Bible's story ends with every nation's people, not their gods, worshipping before God's throne (Rev 7:9-10).

sources.author: John Milton
sources.title: Paradise Lost

callout.text: The detailed hierarchies of demons named after ancient gods (Astaroth, Beelzebub, Moloch) come from medieval magical literature and from Milton, not from the Bible.

views.name: Idols only
views.summary: The other gods were human inventions; the Bible's mockery shows they had no reality beyond wood, stone and imagination.

views.name: Idols with powers behind them
views.summary: The images were nothing, but real spiritual beings (demons or rebellious heavenly powers) stood behind the cults (Deut 32:17; 1 Cor 10:20). This is the common Jewish and Christian view from the Septuagint onward.

views.name: Historical-critical
views.summary: Many of these gods were part of Israel's own religious world before monotheism became dominant; the Bible records the struggle that separated Yahweh from them.

furtherQuestions: If Yahweh took over Baal's storm imagery, does that make him a borrowed god, or a God who claims what false gods were credited with?
Why did the prophets find mockery such an effective weapon against idolatry?
How should we weigh popular religion (figurines, inscriptions) against the official faith of the Bible?
Were the old gods nothing, or demons, or both?
What are the modern equivalents of looking to Baal for rain?

title: The divine council
question: What is the 'divine council' that some scholars find in the Bible? Which passages describe it, what does the Deuteronomy 32:8 variant change, and how strong are the objections and alternative readings?
plainAnswer: Several Bible passages picture God as a king holding court in heaven, surrounded by heavenly beings who stand before him, discuss, and carry out his decisions (1 Kgs 22:19-23; Job 1:6; Ps 82; Dan 7:9-10). Many scholars call this the 'divine council'. Some, especially Michael Heiser, build a whole-Bible story from it: God's council, rebellions by some of its members, the nations placed under lesser 'sons of God' after Babel (Deut 32:8, in its Qumran form), and Jesus reclaiming the nations from those powers. Others accept the council scenes but read key texts differently: the 'gods' of Psalm 82 as human judges, the 'sons of God' in Genesis 6 as Sethites or kings, 'Let us make man' as the Trinity or a plural of majesty, and the Hebrew 'sons of Israel' in Deut 32:8 as original. Critical historians see the council as a remnant of older Canaanite religion. All of these views agree that the Bible presents one God who alone is Creator and alone deserves worship.
keyTakeaways: Heavenly court scenes are clearly in the Bible: Micaiah's vision, Job's prologue, Isaiah's call, Daniel's throne vision.
'Elohim' can refer to beings other than Israel's God, such as the dead Samuel and foreign gods; what that implies is debated.
Deut 32:8 reads 'sons of Israel' in the traditional Hebrew text but 'sons of God' in a Qumran scroll and the Greek tradition; many modern translations follow the latter.
The 'three rebellions' (Eden, Genesis 6, Babel) and 'reclaiming the nations' are a synthesis by some scholars, not a reading all accept.
Alternatives remain strong: human judges in Psalm 82, Sethite or royal readings of Genesis 6, Trinitarian or majestic readings of 'Let us'.
No mainstream view treats council members as gods to be worshipped; the debate is about what kinds of beings exist and how the texts describe them.

sections.heading: The council in plain words
sections.body:
Ancient people often pictured their chief god as a king with a court. At Ugarit, the high god El presides over 'the assembly of El' and 'the sons of El' on a mountain. Babylonian texts describe the gods meeting to decide destinies. The Bible uses similar pictures. God sits on a throne with 'all the host of heaven standing by him' (1 Kgs 22:19); the 'sons of God' come to present themselves before him (Job 1:6); he is 'greatly to be feared in the assembly of the saints' (Ps 89:7); in Daniel's vision 'thousand thousands ministered unto him… the judgment was set, and the books were opened' (Dan 7:10).

The differences matter as much as the similarities. In the Bible, God does not need advice and is never outvoted. The council beings are his creatures (Neh 9:6; Ps 148:2-5) and his servants. They report, praise, volunteer and carry out tasks. Prophets claim to have 'stood in the counsel of the LORD' and so to speak his word (Jer 23:18; Jer 23:22).

The phrase 'divine council' is a scholarly label. Some scholars use it simply for these court scenes. Others, especially in recent evangelical teaching, make it a key to the whole Bible. This guide sets out the texts and the main ways they are read.

sources.author: E. Theodore Mullen Jr.
sources.title: The Assembly of the Gods

sources.author: H. Wheeler Robinson
sources.title: The Council of Yahweh (Journal of Theological Studies 45)

sections.heading: 'Elohim': one word, several uses
sections.body:
The Hebrew word elohim is plural in form but usually means 'God' when it refers to Israel's God, which it does about 2,500 times. Yet the same word is used of other beings. Foreign gods are elohim: Chemosh is the elohim of Moab (Judg 11:24). The medium at Endor sees the dead Samuel as 'elohim ascending out of the earth' (1 Sam 28:13). Psalm 82 says God judges 'among the elohim'. Psalm 8:5 says humans were made 'a little lower than elohim', which the Greek translation and Heb 2:7 render 'angels'. Some older translations take elohim in Exod 22:8-9 as 'judges'.

Divine-council scholars such as Michael Heiser conclude that elohim describes a kind of being whose proper home is the spiritual world, not a set of divine attributes. On this view, 'Yahweh is an elohim, but no other elohim is Yahweh': he alone is uncreated, all-powerful and worthy of worship. Others think this goes too far. They argue that the word's wide use is simply flexible language, as English 'god' can be used of a celebrity or a belly (Phil 3:19), and that biblical writers increasingly deny that other gods are real (Isa 44:9; Jer 10:10-11).

Both sides agree that the Bible never treats other elohim as equal to Yahweh. He is 'God of gods' (Deut 10:17), 'great King above all gods' (Ps 95:3), and the one before whom all gods bow (Ps 97:7).

callout.text: Heiser's description of elohim as a 'place of residence' term is his own proposal. Many scholars accept that the word covers various spiritual beings but do not adopt that definition.

sections.heading: The council scenes
sections.body:
The clearest council scene is Micaiah's vision before Ahab's last battle. Micaiah sees the LORD on his throne with the host of heaven on both sides. God asks who will entice Ahab to his death; various beings make suggestions, and a spirit volunteers to be a lying spirit in the prophets' mouths (1 Kgs 22:19-23). In Job's prologue the 'sons of God' present themselves, and among them comes 'the satan', literally 'the accuser', who questions Job's motives (Job 1:6-12; Job 2:1-6). Hebrew has the definite article ('the accuser'), so many scholars think this is a title for a court official rather than a personal name; how this figure relates to the later Satan is debated.

Isaiah sees the Lord enthroned, surrounded by seraphim, and hears him ask, 'Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?' (Isa 6:1-8). Psalm 89 praises God in 'the congregation of the saints' (Ps 89:5-7). The king of Babylon boasts that he will sit on 'the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north' (Isa 14:13), echoing the language of a divine mountain. In Daniel's vision thrones are set, the court sits, and 'one like the Son of man' comes with the clouds to receive dominion over all nations (Dan 7:9-14). Jesus applies this to himself at his trial (Mark 14:62). In Revelation God's throne is surrounded by twenty-four elders on thrones and living creatures (Rev 4:2-11).

Psalm 82 is the most debated scene: God judges 'among the gods' and sentences them to die like men. Whether those 'gods' are heavenly beings, human judges or Israel at Sinai is discussed in its own debate.

sections.heading: 'Let us make man'
sections.body:
Three times in Genesis God speaks in the plural: 'Let us make man in our image' (Gen 1:26); 'the man is become as one of us' (Gen 3:22); 'let us go down, and there confound their language' (Gen 11:7). Isaiah's 'who will go for us?' (Isa 6:8) is similar. Readers have explained this in four main ways.

The council reading says God is addressing his heavenly court, announcing a decision in which they share as witnesses, though God alone creates (Gen 1:27 returns to the singular: 'God created'). Many Jewish interpreters, including Rashi, read 1:26 this way, as do many modern scholars. The Trinitarian reading, common among the Church Fathers, sees a hint of the plurality within the one God, later revealed as Father, Son and Spirit (John 1:1-3; Col 1:16). The plural of majesty reading compares a king's royal 'we', though critics note that this usage is not clearly attested in biblical Hebrew. The plural of deliberation reading sees God speaking to himself, as a person says 'let's see'.

These options are not all exclusive. Some Christian interpreters hold that the original setting is a council address, while the fuller meaning in the light of the New Testament is Trinitarian.

callout.text: The council reading does not say angels created humans or share God's image-giving power. Its defenders stress that Gen 1:27 attributes creation to God alone.

sections.heading: Deuteronomy 32:8 and the nations
sections.body:
The Song of Moses says that when the Most High divided the nations, 'he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel. For the LORD's portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance' (Deut 32:8-9). That is the reading of the traditional Hebrew text (the Masoretic Text), followed by the KJV, NASB and NIV.

But a Hebrew manuscript of Deuteronomy found at Qumran (4QDeut-j, from Cave 4, discovered in 1952) reads 'sons of God' (bene elohim). The Greek Septuagint reads 'angels of God' in most manuscripts and 'sons of God' in some. Many textual scholars think 'sons of God' is original and that a later scribe changed it to 'sons of Israel', perhaps because it seemed to suggest many gods. The harder reading is often the original one, and 'sons of Israel' makes poor sense, since Israel did not yet exist when the nations were divided (Gen 10–11). The RSV, NRSV, ESV and NET follow the Qumran and Greek reading in some form.

On the council reading, this verse explains a lot: after Babel God allotted the nations to lesser heavenly beings and kept Israel for himself. That is why Deuteronomy says God 'divided' the sun, moon and stars to the nations (Deut 4:19) and speaks of gods 'whom he had not given unto them' (Deut 29:26), and why Daniel mentions heavenly 'princes' of Persia and Greece (Dan 10:13; Dan 10:20). Others accept 'sons of God' but take them simply as angels who serve God among the nations, or argue that the Masoretic reading reflects a genuine tradition linking the nations to Israel's seventy members (Gen 46:27; Exod 1:5).

sources.author: Emanuel Tov
sources.title: Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible

sources.author: Michael S. Heiser
sources.title: Deuteronomy 32:8 and the Sons of God (Bibliotheca Sacra 158)

sections.heading: Three rebellions? A synthesis and its critics
sections.body:
Some divine-council writers, Heiser especially, read Genesis 1–11 as three rebellions by heavenly beings that explain the state of the world. First, Eden: the serpent (nachash) is a council member who deceives humanity and is cursed (Gen 3:1-15); Christians identify him with Satan (Rev 12:9; Rev 20:2). Heiser's suggestion that nachash also plays on 'diviner' and 'shining one' is a word-play many scholars think is unlikely. Second, Genesis 6: the 'sons of God' cross into the human world and father the Nephilim (Gen 6:1-4), echoed in Jude 1:6 and 2 Pet 2:4. Third, Babel: humanity unites against God, and God scatters the nations and places them under the 'sons of God' (Gen 11:1-9; Deut 32:8), some of whom then rule badly and become the nations' gods (Ps 82).

This reading has real strengths: it connects passages that are often treated in isolation, and it explains why the New Testament speaks of 'principalities' and 'powers' (Eph 6:12; Col 2:15). But each link is debated. The serpent is not called a council member in Genesis. Genesis 6 has strong human readings (Sethites, royal tyrants). Babel does not mention the sons of God. And much of the detail comes from Second Temple books such as 1 Enoch, which, though old and influential, are not part of most Christian Bibles.

A fair summary is that the three-rebellion story is an interpretive synthesis. It is held by a growing number of evangelical teachers, but it is not the consensus of biblical scholars, and many careful readers prefer to keep the Bible's own statements and the synthesis distinct.

sources.author: Michael S. Heiser
sources.title: The Unseen Realm

sources.author: Archie T. Wright
sources.title: The Origin of Evil Spirits: The Reception of Genesis 6:1-4 in Early Jewish Literature

sections.heading: Reclaiming the nations
sections.body:
Whatever one makes of the council, the Bible clearly tells a story in which God, who chose Israel, intends to bring all nations back. Abraham is called so that 'all families of the earth' will be blessed (Gen 12:3). Psalm 82 ends, 'Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations' (Ps 82:8). Daniel's Son of Man receives a kingdom 'that all people, nations, and languages, should serve him' (Dan 7:14). The risen Jesus says all authority is his and sends his followers to 'all nations' (Matt 28:18-19).

Council readers add detail. Pentecost, where people from many nations hear God's works in their own languages (Acts 2:5-11), reverses Babel's confusion of languages. Some scholars, such as James M. Scott, argue that Luke's list of nations and Paul's plans echo the Table of Nations in Genesis 10; this is a debated hypothesis. Paul describes Christ disarming 'principalities and powers' (Col 2:15) and the church making God's wisdom known to them (Eph 3:10). He calls former gods those 'which by nature are no gods' (Gal 4:8) and plans to go as far as Spain (Rom 15:24; Rom 15:28), which some link to Tarshish, the far west of the known world (Isa 66:19), though the identification of Tarshish is itself uncertain.

The end of the story is a renewed council. In Revelation the Lamb is worthy because he redeemed people 'out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation' (Rev 5:9), the nations walk in the light of the city (Rev 21:24), and the leaves of the tree are 'for the healing of the nations' (Rev 22:2). Believers are called God's sons (Rom 8:14; Gal 3:26), will judge angels (1 Cor 6:3) and will reign with Christ (Rev 3:21; Rev 22:5).

sources.author: James M. Scott
sources.title: Paul and the Nations

sections.heading: Objections and alternatives
sections.body:
Is this polytheism? Council defenders say no: the council beings are created (Col 1:16), subordinate and even mortal (Ps 82:7), and only Yahweh is worshipped. Classical monotheists reply that the Bible's strongest statements go beyond 'no rival': 'there is no God beside me' (Isa 45:5) and idols are 'nothing' (Isa 41:24). Council defenders answer that Babylon and Nineveh use the same 'none beside me' phrase of themselves (Isa 47:8; Zeph 2:15), so it means incomparability; many scholars, however, still read Second Isaiah as explicit monotheism. Paul holds both together: idols are nothing, yet demons are real (1 Cor 8:4-6; 1 Cor 10:19-21).

For particular texts, the alternatives are serious. Psalm 82's 'gods' have long been read as human judges (Calvin, Rashi) or as Israel at Sinai (rabbinic tradition), readings that fit Jesus' use in John 10 well. The 'sons of God' in Genesis 6 have been read as Sethites (Augustine, Calvin) or as kings (Targums, Kline). 'Let us' has Trinitarian and majestic readings. Deut 32:8 has a defensible traditional text. Critical historians such as Mark S. Smith accept that the council texts describe divine beings but see them as remnants of Israel's older, polytheistic religion, not as a consistent biblical theology.

There is also a practical objection. Popular teaching on territorial spirits, spiritual mapping or hidden giants can grow out of council language far beyond what the texts say. Responsible defenders of the council reading warn against this as strongly as their critics do.

sources.author: Mark S. Smith
sources.title: The Origins of Biblical Monotheism

sources.author: Richard Bauckham
sources.title: Jesus and the God of Israel

callout.text: Myth: 'The divine council view says Christians should honour lesser gods.' Fact: no defender teaches that. The view is about what beings exist; worship belongs to God alone (Exod 20:3; Rev 22:8-9).

sections.heading: What this means for reading the Bible
sections.body:
Whatever view you take, the council passages remind readers that the Bible's world is larger than the visible one. Prayer, worship and mission are pictured as happening before a heavenly court (Heb 12:22-24; Rev 5:8-14). The struggle against evil is described not only as human politics but as a struggle against spiritual powers (Eph 6:12), which is a reason for humility and prayer rather than fear or speculation.

The passages also keep returning to justice. Psalm 82's rulers are condemned for neglecting the poor and fatherless (Ps 82:3-4), whoever they are. The nations' gods fail because they cannot save (Isa 45:20). The Son of Man's kingdom is everlasting and just (Dan 7:14).

Finally, the council texts show that the Bible's confession of one God is not thin. God is not lonely or abstract; he is the King of a vast creation, surrounded by worshipping beings, who chooses to share his rule with redeemed humans (Rev 3:21). Christians read this, in the end, through Jesus, who has 'gone into heaven, and is on the right hand of God; angels and authorities and powers being made subject unto him' (1 Pet 3:22).

views.name: Divine-council synthesis
views.summary: The council is a key biblical theme: created divine beings, rebellions, nations under rebel powers, and Christ reclaiming the nations (Heiser and others).

views.name: Council scenes without the synthesis
views.summary: The court scenes are real and important, but texts like Ps 82, Gen 6 and Gen 1:26 have other good readings; the 'three rebellions' story goes beyond the evidence.

views.name: Classical monotheism
views.summary: Heavenly beings are angels; 'gods' language is poetic or refers to idols and rulers; the Bible teaches that only one God exists.

views.name: Historical-critical
views.summary: The council is inherited from Canaanite religion and reflects an earlier stage of Israelite belief before full monotheism (Mark S. Smith and others).
